rows.title: A deadly fire exposes the lack of protection for migrant workers in South Korea
rows.standfirst: As South Korea's population shrinks, foreign migrant workers are joining the country's workforce. But a recent deadly fire exposed the risks some of them are facing.

rows.title: One of the hottest jobs in AI right now: 'types-question guy'
rows.standfirst: U.S. job growth cooled this month. But one job is hot to the touch: AI prompt engineer. The role can command a six figure salary, but ... what is it? Today, we speak to an AI prompt engineer to figure out what they actually do and how long the job could remain hot.

rows.title: How flying got so bad (or did it?)
rows.standfirst: We often hear that air travel is worse than it's ever been. Gone are the days when airplanes touted piano bars and meat carving stations — or even free meals. Instead we're crammed into tiny seats and fighting for overhead space.

rows.title: Courts, regulators tackle whether 'sale-leaseback' deals are actually loans
rows.standfirst: Courts are tackling the question of whether sale-leaseback deals function more like a mortgage than an outright sale — and therefore should be regulated like a loan.

rows.title: Amazon is 30. Here's how a book store gobbled up all of e-commerce
rows.standfirst: Jeff Bezos founded the e-commerce giant in his garage 30 years ago. NPR's Andrew Mambo talks with business reporter Alina Selyukh about how Bezos built an empire and what's next for the company.

rows.title: Greece's new 6-day workweek law takes effect, bucking a trend
rows.standfirst: An employee who must work on a sixth day would be paid 40% overtime, according to the new law.

rows.title: Luxury department store Saks buys Neiman Marcus, and Amazon gets a stake
rows.standfirst: The two high-end department stores hope together they would wield more power to counter luxury brands, which increasingly flex their muscles over retailers.

rows.title: The two companies driving the modern economy
rows.standfirst: At the core of most of the electronics we use today are some very tiny, very powerful chips. Semiconductor chips. And they are mighty: they help power our phones, laptops, and cars. They enable advances in healthcare, military systems, transportation, and clean energy. And they're also critical for artificial intelligence, providing the hardware needed to train complex machine learning.

rows.title: Jessica Campbell will be the 1st woman on an NHL bench as assistant coach in Seattle
rows.standfirst: Campbell was hired Wednesday for the Kraken, becoming the first woman in an on-the-bench role as an assistant or associate coach in NHL history. She was a decorated player in the NCAA and in Canada.

rows.title: Federal judge partially blocks U.S. ban on noncompetes
rows.standfirst: A federal judge in Texas has partially blocked the government's ban on noncompetes. An estimated 30 million U.S. workers are subject to the employment agreements.

rows.title: The game theory that led to nuclear standoffs
rows.standfirst: Last week, Vladimir Putin vowed to make new nuclear weapons and consider placing them close to NATO countries. Meanwhile, here in the US, the government boosted its nuclear weapon spending by 18% between 2022 and 2023.

rows.title: 'We’re not stuck.' Why Boeing’s Starliner isn’t returning to Earth (yet)
rows.standfirst: The return of Starliner has been indefinitely delayed, but NASA and Boeing say the astronauts will use the spaceship to get home — eventually.

rows.title: The economic implications of Europe's jolt right
rows.standfirst: Europe is expecting a wave of victories from far-right candidates in upcoming national elections. Voters are showing they're worried about income inequality, immigration and the effects of participating in a global economy. Today, we take a look at what the swing to the right means for Europe's economy and the European stance on globalization.

rows.title: Dining out with a big group? Learn the social etiquette of splitting the check
rows.standfirst: Five common scenarios you may encounter while dining out with a large party — and how to handle the bill fairly while being considerate of your server.

rows.title: America's startup boom is still going strong. Here's what it means for the economy
rows.standfirst: Four years ago, Americans began creating new businesses at a record rate. The boom is still here, and it could be a great sign for the U.S. economy.

rows.title: Food prices are no longer rising as much — but here's why it might not feel that way
rows.standfirst: Food prices have largely leveled off, but many people are still frustrated when they go to their local grocery store.

rows.title: EU takes Elon Musk's X to court over blue checks and ads
rows.standfirst: The European Union has charged Elon Musk’s X with violating new regulations for social media platforms. Musk faces hefty fines over delivering misinformation.

rows.title: Rooftop solar's dark side
rows.standfirst: 4.5 million households in the U.S. have solar panels on their homes. Most of those customers are happy with it - their electricity bills have just about disappeared, and it's great for the planet. But thousands and thousands of people are really disappointed with what they've been sold. Their panels are more expensive than they should be, and they say it is hard to get someone to come fix them when they break.

rows.title: Greece allows a 6-day work week and other indicators
rows.standfirst: On Indicators of the Week, we cover the numbers in the news that you should know about. This week, we cover an encouraging trend for global wealth, closing Mexico's tariff loophole and the European nation bucking the trend of shorter work weeks.

rows.title: AT&T says hackers stole 2022 call and text data from 'nearly all' cell customers
rows.standfirst: AT&T believes the data, which was stolen in April, is no longer publicly available. Affected current and former customers will be notified by the company but can also check their status online.

rows.title: AI brings soaring emissions for Google and Microsoft, a major contributor to climate change
rows.standfirst: The tech giants both report surges in greenhouse gas emissions as they double-down on adding artificial intelligence to all of their products.

rows.title: An asylum seeker's long road to a work permit
rows.standfirst: There are currently just under 65,000 migrants in New York City's shelter system, stretching the city's outworn social service systems. Today on the show, we follow one asylum seeker's journey from Venezuela to New York and explore why the process is lengthy and complicated.

rows.title: Marathon Oil reaches a $241 million settlement with EPA for environmental violations
rows.standfirst: The federal government announced a settlement with Marathon Oil for alleged air quality violations at the company's oil and gas operations on the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation in North Dakota.

rows.title: Philadelphia workers have to show up in the office today, flying birds or not
rows.standfirst: The City of Philadelphia has ordered all city workers to return to the office five days a week starting July 15. A judge ruled the mandate could go forward, despite opposition from union workers.

rows.title: NPR gets $5.5 million grant to strengthen local journalism as news deserts spread
rows.standfirst: The grant, from Eric and Wendy Schmidt, will be used to launch regional newsrooms in Appalachia and the Mountain West. It will also be used to strengthen existing public media collaboratives in New England, the Midwest and California.

rows.title: History 1: Money and the stone coin at the bottom of the sea
rows.standfirst: Planet Money Summer School is back for eight weeks. Join as we travel back in time to find the origins of our economic way of life. Today we ask surprisingly hard question: What is money? And where did it come from? We travel to a remote island in the Pacific Ocean for the answer. Then we'll visit France in the year 1714, where a man on the lam tries to revolutionize the country's entire monetary system, and comes impressively close to the modern economy we have today, before it all falls apart. Check out our Summer School video cheat sheet on the origins of money at the Planet Money TikTok.

rows.title: Bread and bullets: Some Southern supermarkets now sell ammo out of vending machines
rows.standfirst: American Rounds has installed machines at eight stores so far, with hundreds more on the way. It says this is the safest way to sell ammo, but cyber and gun violence prevention experts have concerns.

rows.title: What has helped you afford housing in this market? We want to hear from you
rows.standfirst: Record numbers of Americans face unaffordable rent and home prices. If you’re among them, please tell us about the sacrifices or creative solutions this has meant for you.

rows.title: BMW recalling more than 390,000 vehicles due to airbag inflator issue
rows.standfirst: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said the recall includes certain 3 Series Sedans and 3 Series Sportswagons. BMW dealers will inspect and replace air bag modules as needed for free.

rows.title: How much do presidents ACTUALLY influence the economy?
rows.standfirst: Voters have a bleak outlook on the economy right now, and many are pointing the finger at President Biden. At the same time, many voters have a rosy view of the economy when Donald Trump was president. But how much credit or blame should a president get for the economy? And how do partisan politics play into our perception of the economy's performance?

rows.title: American Airlines reaches agreement with flight attendant union, avoiding strike
rows.standfirst: At the center of the deal is a proposed new contract for about 28,000 workers which includes increased pay levels. Flight attendants had not received salary increases since 2019.

rows.title: Disruptions continue after IT outage affects millions around the globe
rows.standfirst: Airports, hospitals, and banks said they were recovering after a failed software update delivered by the cybersecurity company CrowdStrike to Microsoft’s Windows systems.

rows.title: The company that owns colors
rows.standfirst: In 2022, artist Stuart Semple opened up his laptop to find that all his designs had turned black overnight. All the colors, across files on Adobe products like Photoshop and Illustrator, were gone. Who had taken the colors away? The story of what happened begins with one company, Pantone.

rows.title: Bankruptcy, basketball, and bringing the dollar down
rows.standfirst: It's Indicators of the Week! We cover the numbers in the news that you should know about. This week, we cover climbing corporate bankruptcies, J.D. Vance's potential to bring the dollar down, and the NBA's new super serious salary cap.

rows.title: Netflix ends its cheapest ad-free subscription
rows.standfirst: Netflix says it will no longer offer its basic plan for U.S. and French subscribers, which had already been phased out of other markets.

rows.title: Soda cans are exploding on Southwest flights due to sky-high temperatures
rows.standfirst: The extreme heat searing the U.S. this summer is having an unexpected consequence thousands of feet in the air: It's causing some beverage cans on Southwest Airlines flights to burst when opened.

rows.title: Russian court sentences U.S. journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in prison
rows.standfirst: A Russian court convicted Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich on charges of espionage Friday, sentencing him to 16 years in a Russian prison colony in a trial the U.S. denounced as a sham.

rows.title: What we know about the computer update glitch disrupting systems around the world
rows.standfirst: A tech meltdown left workers at airlines, banks and hospitals staring at the dreaded “blue screen of death” as their computers went inert in what is being described as a historic outage.

rows.title: Lou Dobbs, the controversial Fox News host, has died
rows.standfirst: The longtime Fox contributor was 78 years old.

rows.title: Goodbye, Chevron. Hello, lawsuits!
rows.standfirst: The Supreme Court's decision to quash Chevron deference means countless agency regulations are now more vulnerable to being challenged and struck down. Think the Environmental Protection Agency's plan to boost electric vehicle sales, discrimination protections against transgender people, and rules that expand eligibility for overtime.

rows.title: Home insurance rates are rising due to climate change. What could break that cycle?
rows.standfirst: A warming planet is making storms and wildfires more intense, and more destructive. That's making homeowners insurance more expensive and harder to find.

rows.title: 35,000 more public servants see their student loan balances reduced or erased
rows.standfirst: The Biden administration announced $1.2 billion in student loan forgiveness for borrowers who work in public service, including as firefighters, social workers and teachers.

rows.title: Too toxic for Fox News, Tucker Carlson snags a key role at GOP convention
rows.standfirst: Fox News founder Rupert Murdoch has been considered a kingmaker in Republican circles. Now two men he shunned — former President Donald Trump and former Fox star Tucker Carlson — are in the spotlight.

rows.title: You can pan for gold at Wall Drug in South Dakota. Locals need it as a pharmacy, too
rows.standfirst: Wall Drug is a huge, cowboy-themed tourist attraction near Badlands National Park, visited by 2 million people a year. It also has a functional pharmacy that faces many of the challenges of rural health care.

rows.title: Five things to know about J.D. Vance’s ties to tech billionaires
rows.standfirst: Vance, who has become a darling to the Silicon Valley elite, made inroads in tech and venture capital circles during a stint in San Francisco. Now, Vance is tapping that network to supercharge the Trump re-election bid.

rows.title: Are both rents AND interest rates too dang high?
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve has once again opted to leave interest rates unchanged. That appears to be creating a big challenge to one part of the economy: housing prices. Today, we look at how elevated interest rates may actually be keeping home prices and rent high. Plus, we see how one community is taking the issue of housing affordability into its own hands.

rows.title: U.K. police reviewing accusations against 'Washington Post' publisher
rows.standfirst: British police are reviewing allegations that Washington Post CEO Will Lewis obstructed justice when he worked for media mogul Rupert Murdoch in the U.K. 13 years ago.

rows.title: History 4: Banker vs president and the birth of the dollar
rows.standfirst: Episodes each Wednesday through labor day. Find all the episodes from this season here. And past seasons here. And follow along on TikTok here for video Summer School.

rows.title: Trump attacks Kamala Harris’ racial identity at Black journalism convention
rows.standfirst: Donald Trump falsely questioned Kamala Harris' racial identity Wednesday, saying that in the past she only promoted her Indian heritage until, he said, "she happened to turn Black."

rows.title: Summer School 4: Banker vs president and the birth of the dollar
rows.standfirst: Episodes each Wednesday through labor day. Find all the episodes from this season here. And past seasons here. And follow along on TikTok here for video Summer School.

rows.title: The Federal Reserve is getting closer to cutting interest rates
rows.standfirst: The Fed kept interest rates unchanged at the highest in more than two decades. Investors are betting it will start to lower rates at its next meeting in September.

rows.title: Illinois bans companies from forcing workers to listen to their anti-union talk
rows.standfirst: Illinois is the 8th state to adopt a law making it illegal for employers to hold mandatory religious, political or anti-union meetings, a move aimed at helping workers trying to unionize.

rows.title: Delta's CEO says the CrowdStrike outage cost the airline $500 million in 5 days
rows.standfirst: The airline's CEO, Ed Bastian, says the massive tech outage that stranded countless passengers cost the airline a half-billion dollars. The carrier is now preparing litigation against CrowdStrike, he said.

rows.title: Boeing names aerospace veteran Kelly Ortberg as its next CEO
rows.standfirst: The struggling planemaker says Ortberg will take over next week as Dave Calhoun departs. The news came as Boeing reported disappointing second-quarter earnings, with losses of more than $1.4 billion.

rows.title: Do you rent? You may be more vulnerable to climate-driven disasters
rows.standfirst: The financial cards are stacked against many renters who survive hurricanes, floods, wildfires and other major weather disasters. The long-term effects can be devastating.

rows.title: Ex-NFL star Terrell Davis and United offer differing accounts of his ban from airline
rows.standfirst: The Hall of Famer says he's been banned from future United Airlines flights after an incident earlier this month. But the airline says the ban was lifted almost immediately.

rows.title: Trump's planned address to Black journalists convention sparks backlash
rows.standfirst: Former President Donald Trump will address journalists at the NABJ convention in Chicago. Many, however, have questioned the decision to offer a platform to the Republican nominee.

rows.title: Test your knowledge of NVIDIA, ChatGPT and...Peppa Pig?
rows.standfirst: It's time for The Indicator Quiz!

rows.title: Paris Olympics TV ratings are up 79% over Tokyo Games, NBC says
rows.standfirst: Some of the ratings growth could be explained by a more U.S.-friendly time zone difference. Then there's the joy: Athletes aren't required to wear masks, and fans are allowed in the stands.

rows.title: Ozempic's biggest side effect: Turning Denmark into a 'pharmastate'?
rows.standfirst: Novo Nordisk is powering Denmark's economy with huge sales of Ozempic. But could its stratospheric growth pose a risk?
